title: Ask HN: Where has creativity in software gone?
summary:
I sometimes read Show HN, and there is literally no creativity at all: note-taker app after note-taker clone. Everyone is essentially looking at what’s already there, and they say, “Why can’t I create the exact same product, but worse, and add an AI suffix?”

There is nothing creative about AI. Show HN might as well be renamed “Prompt HN.” These promoters always say, “Prompting makes me efficient; I don’t have to write code by hand anymore.”

Great. What has your “efficiency” gotten you? Yet another note-taker with an “AI” suffix? I could take notes in 1990.

Where did the actual engineers go? Surely they aren’t all selling ads at Facebook’s spyware empire? Where are the transistor, the C programming language, Emacs, and SQLite developers of our time?

title: Ask HN: How long before someone reverse-engineers Windows?
summary:
It just occurred to me that similar to Photoshop suite, someone is already working on getting Windows 10/11 reverse-engineered in a clean-room fashion.

I don't want to get into the discussion over the whole Craft suite, it's already been the talk of past week, after all, but judging by the pure popularity and the number of merge requests created within those couple days for just their Photoshop equivalent app, I am guessing these projects are not* going away anytime soon and they will, in fact, polish-out majority of issues: https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/pulls

Also, while the original authors claim it was done without the debugger, I am absolutely certain thousands have their LLMs actively analyzing Adobe Suite now to get understand the knicks and crannies of it.

So if people hating on Adobe flocked to contribute to this project so enthusiastically, I guess we can only imagine the sheer amount of interest worldwide an open-source Windows would bring, and not only from the volunteers this time around..

title: Tell HN: ChatGPT on macOS grants local computer access to cloud account
summary:
I recently started a conversation on ChatGPT for macOS in "Work" mode with the "In the Cloud" execution option enabled. I was expecting this to run on a cloud VM, just like "Work" conversations started on chatgpt.com

When I continued it in the browser (e.g. via right clicking it on macOS and then selecting "Open on chatgpt.com"), I was pretty shocked to learn that it actually had (and still has) access to my local file system. I could just prompt it to list files in my home directory, in /Applications etc.

I never have opted into this behavior in the macOS app, nor does there seem to be any way to deactivate it. It's somewhat documented for enterprise accounts [1], and it can be deactivated for those in the admin panel, but this seems like the wrong place: Why should this be possible to activate remotely?

Can anybody confirm this behavior? Maybe I'm missing something, but this seems pretty concerning.

[1] https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/enterprise/cloud-local-access

Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50078284

title: Tell HN: Free Refills with This Tumbler
summary:
Background: At this point in my life, I roll out of bed and get coffee from Dunkin'. Large, black, hot. It's like $4. I'm not happy about it, but I swipe and go on with my day.

The bagel shop I go to has a $15 tumbler that you can get free refills with. I love this because a cup of coffee anywhere is like $3 and it's all margin. My new routine is go there, get a bagel with a spread for like $4 and get coffee.

I'm ahead cause now I have coffee and food. They're ahead because they're not even trying to compete with coffee shops. They just give away the free stuff. I've made my money back on the tumbler and they keep making $4/day off me.

What's the software equivalent?

Differences: coffee has non-zero cost everywhere. software has zero cost with ads. If I give away coffee, that brings people to my store. If I give away software, will people buy something to go with the free software?

title: Ask HN: Are signed URL previews feasible?
summary:
Lots of protocols and software allow URL previews. But they have some annoying limitations:

For centralized public services the server can just retrieve the preview and serve it. But for decentralized services like Mastodon either every server has to fetch the preview on its own leading to lots of traffic and potential discrepancies between the previews served by different servers or the origin home server sends the preview but now everyone has to trust that it is authentic. The home server to which a link gets posted could place anything as its preview and thereby indirectly impersonate the URL and fake its content.

For E2EE messengers things are even more annoying because you do not want the servers to see the URL at all. So either all parties have to retrieve the preview on their own meaning they have to connect to a random, potentially malicious URL or only the sender does and everyone has to trust the sender that the preview is authentic which is a great opportunity for scams.^1

The perfect solution would be a standard for web servers to sign URL previews with their CA issued certificate. So that you can always proof that a preview is authentic. RFC 9421 already standardizes this. But this will not happen. There is virtually no chance of widespread adoption.

So my idea is:

You retrieve a webpage and record the whole TLS session including certificates, MACs and your key material like nonce and client random from the handshake. Now you use this as the basis for the URL preview. When you include your secret material from the TLS handshake anyone should be able to verify that the content is authentic from the server serving the URL due to the CA certificate and authentication of TLS traffic.

Standardize the request headers and limit the response length. Just cut off everything after the limit. Define some algorithm for computing the preview that ever recipient can verify. If you want to include linked images in the preview that increases complexity but should be doable. Repeat the whole thing with the linked image and create a bundle from all requests that authenticates the preview.

The downside I see is complexity and the need for the receiver to parse the preview bundle which might be attack surface.

Does anything similar already exist? Am I missing something or do you think this might be feasible to implement?

[1] Many messengers solve this by providing a URL preview service on the server. The client sends the URL to the messenger service which retrieves (and signs I hope) a URL preview which the client then includes in the message. This has the advantage that none of the parties of the conversation has to directly connect to an untrusted UTL. This bypasses E2EE for URLs. You can usually opt of this by disabling previews. Consider this if you did not know about this.

title: Ask HN: How bad Earth would have to be for terraforming Mars to make sense?
summary:
Ok, this might be more of a Reddit question or an xkcd’s “What if”, but let’s try here first.

When people talk about investing in tech so that, if Earth gets bad enough, we have a plan B in colonizing Mars, I think we most agree that it’s nonsense. But it seems like a good thought experiment.

What would have to happen to Earth so that, given we have developed the technology, terraforming Mars and moving some people there is a sensible option?

Mars having no water, no atmosphere, and no organic matter make it a high bar.

I believe global nuclear war or the worst predictions of climate change won’t cut it. A meteor, not if it is the same size the one that already hit Earth and wasn’t enough to kill all life, much less remove atmosphere or water.

So, what is this scenario where putting the resources (again, given we have the tech) to create a colony on Mars make sense?
